subject: physics
title: Energy levels and line spectra
key_idea: Electrons in an isolated atom can only have certain energies. When an electron drops to a lower level, the atom emits a photon with exactly the difference in energy. That is why atoms give line spectra, not a smooth rainbow.

blocks.text: An atom's electrons can only have certain fixed energies, called energy levels. The levels are discrete, so energies in between are not allowed.

items.meaning: The lowest energy level of an atom.
An electron moves to a higher energy level, taking energy from a photon or a collision.
An electron gains enough energy to leave the atom completely.

items: Energy levels have negative values. Zero is the energy of a free electron at rest, outside the atom.
The more negative the level, the more tightly bound the electron.
Ionisation energy is the energy needed to take an electron from the ground state to zero energy.
Energy levels are quoted in joules or in eV. Convert with 1 eV = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.

blocks.text: An electron colliding with an atom can excite or ionise it if it has enough kinetic energy. A photon must have exactly the right energy to excite an electron.

items: Electron energies in an atom are discrete.
Levels are negative; ionisation reaches zero.

blocks.text: When an electron falls from a higher level E₁ to a lower level E₂, the atom emits one photon. The photon carries away the difference in energy.

blocks.label: Photon from a transition
where: E₁, E₂ = upper and lower energy levels (J)

items: A bigger energy gap gives a higher frequency and a shorter wavelength.
Absorption is the reverse: a photon is absorbed only if hf equals the gap between two levels.
Photons whose energy matches no gap (and is below the ionisation energy) pass through without being absorbed.

diagram.alt: A slider for hydrogen energy level transitions. Choose a transition and read the photon energy, frequency and wavelength.

items: Photon energy equals the difference between two levels: hf = E₁ − E₂.
Only certain photon energies are possible, so only certain frequencies.

blocks.text: A spectrum shows the wavelengths present in light. There are three kinds.

rows: A smooth band of all colours
Hot solid, liquid or dense gas emits all wavelengths
Bright coloured lines on a dark background
A hot, low-pressure gas emits photons as electrons fall between levels
Dark lines across a continuous spectrum
Cool gas in front of a continuous source absorbs photons that match its energy gaps

items: The dark lines in an absorption spectrum are at the same wavelengths as the bright lines in the emission spectrum of the same gas.
Each element has its own pattern of lines, because each has its own energy levels. Line spectra are evidence for discrete energy levels.
The lines in light from a star identify the elements in its atmosphere.
A line spectrum is evidence for discrete energy levels.
Absorption lines match the emission lines of the same element.

checks.q: State what is meant by an excited atom.
checks.a: An atom in which an electron is in a higher energy level than the ground state.

checks.q: An electron falls from an energy level of −1.5 eV to one of −3.4 eV. Calculate the wavelength of the photon emitted. (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s, e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
Explain why an absorption spectrum has dark lines.
checks.a: Atoms in a cool gas absorb photons whose energy equals the gap between two of their levels. Those wavelengths are removed from the continuous spectrum, leaving dark lines.

blocks.text: A fluorescent tube shows ionisation and excitation at work.

items.text: A high voltage accelerates electrons through mercury vapour in the tube.
The atoms fall back and emit ultraviolet photons.
A fluorescent coating on the tube absorbs the ultraviolet and re-emits visible light.

items: Some collisions ionise the mercury atoms, which keeps the tube conducting.
Without the coating the tube would give out mostly ultraviolet.
Collisions excite and ionise the gas.
The coating turns ultraviolet into visible light.
